extracted.intended_audience: general readers / students of Montaigne and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Michel de Montaigne's Essays (early modern moral and political reflection) focused on custom, law, innovation, and clemency. The page is a literary/philosophical meditation rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom seizes and ensnares people so strongly that it is hard to disengage oneself from its grip; what is off the hinges of custom is believed to be off the hinges of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that customs are 'sucked in with our milk' and present themselves as the natural posture of the world; he gives many ethnographic examples (distinct and sometimes strange practices of other nations) to show how universally custom shapes belief and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of conscience derive from custom
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of conscience, which are commonly claimed to come from nature, actually proceed from custom and inherited opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because people venerate the opinions and manners received among their own people, they cannot easily depart from them; Montaigne cites examples of family and national usages that become moral standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey the laws of the place where one lives
rubrics_metrics.description: One should observe the laws of the country in which one lives; public obedience to local law is the 'rule of rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne invokes Socrates as an exemplar and quotes 'It is good to obey the laws of one’s country.' He argues for outward conformity to local customs and laws even while keeping private judgment free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against innovation/change of established laws
rubrics_metrics.description: There is great danger and inconvenience in altering received laws because government is a complex, interdependent structure; moving one 'brick or stone' affects the whole body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Charondas' halter rule for innovators, Lacedaemonian oath to preserve laws, the story of Ephoros cutting new musical strings; Montaigne warns innovation often produces public disorder, civil war, and the ruin of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private reason has limited jurisdiction over public institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Private reason is of private jurisdiction and it is unjust to subject public customs and institutions to the whims of a single individual's fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne insists reformers must not impose private judgment on the divine or civil order; those who would change public law should carefully discern defects and virtues rather than follow personal caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators must clearly discern defects and virtues before reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who proposes to abolish an old law or establish a new one must be sure to discern the defect of what they would remove and the virtue of what they would introduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises great caution and responsibility for reformers; he cites Isocrates and other authorities to argue that rash changes are presumptuous and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding the law in urgent necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary necessity or exigent circumstances may justify temporary suspension, alteration, or flexibility in the application of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Agesilaus suspending laws for 24 hours, shifting a calendar day, Alexander making an extra May in June, Lacedaemonians’ adaptations to appoint Lysander; Montaigne allows for measured deviation when public necessity demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clemency/forgiveness as a political tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Clemency and mercy can secure loyalty and prevent further plots; pardoning an implicated conspirator may be both morally and politically effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Augustus pardoning Cinna (turning an enemy into a friend and later benefactor) and the Duc de Guise forgiving a discovered would-be assassin; Montaigne views such acts as prudential as well as humane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty for novelty’s sake
rubrics_metrics.description: A disposition to favour novelty (innovation merely because it is new) is dangerous; novelty often brings unforeseen evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne confesses personal aversion to novelty, arguing that many mischiefs and ruins have been accidentally produced by innovators and that imitators spread these disorders further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate private thought from public conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: One may and should keep inner judgment free while outwardly conforming to the fashions and practices of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne proposes that while a wise man should withdraw his soul from the crowd for internal judgment, he should still follow external fashions to maintain social harmony; examples include dress and public manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation begets imitation and disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who invent new disorders do the greatest harm, but imitators are more vicious because they perpetuate and spread the example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne remarks that inventors create precedents for wicked enterprises and imitators, having felt and punished the horror, still continue the example—citing civil wars and public commotions as consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imitate divine miracles as human precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary divine acts are not to serve as models for human action; they are manifestations of special providence, not rules for ordinary conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that human beings should admire miracles but not attempt to imitate them; such acts are 'masterstrokes of the divine hand' beyond human rule or force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of commodified justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A system in which judicial office and justice are bought and sold is savage and corrupt, producing double standards of honour and law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reproaches nations where judges' offices are merchandise, where justice can be denied for lack of money, and where the law forms a distinct, profit-making fourth estate separate from nobility and clergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation (defect nearer moderation than excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect is nearer allied to moderation than excess; moderation is preferable to the presumption of radical change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Isocrates to support the view that moderation is closer to virtue and that extravagant attempts at reform are rash and potentially ruinous.
